# The graveyard

Source: https://lowob.com/research/the-graveyard/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-15 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: The most valuable thing an organisation knows is what it tried and abandoned, and why. It is also the first thing lost when people move. A judgment system should make the graveyard first-class, and distinguish what was disproven from what was merely under-tried. The research supports both halves: knowledge built through work depreciates quickly, and NASA's own inspector general found that only 57% of project managers surveyed used the agency's lessons-learned system at all.

## Key points

- Every function has a graveyard of abandoned initiatives, and the reasons usually live in the heads of whoever was there.
- Classify each death as disproven, under-tried, overtaken or political, because each has different implications for revival.
- Each record should state what would make the idea worth trying again, turning a tombstone into a reopenable option.
- Archives that wait to be searched go unread; match new proposals to old records and surface the closest one.
- Count repeat failures, which should be zero, and successful revivals.

Every function has a graveyard. The channel that did not work. The pricing model withdrawn after a quarter. The partnership that looked perfect and was quietly ended. The analytics vendor dropped after the pilot. The reasons live in the heads of whoever was there.

When those people move on, a new owner arrives with fresh eyes and, very often, revives one of the abandoned ideas. Sometimes because a vendor pitched it, sometimes because a board member suggested it, sometimes because it simply looks obvious. Occasionally conditions have changed and it works. Often it fails again, for the same reason, at full cost, and nobody connects the two failures.

## How the graveyard gets lost

Three findings explain why the reasons disappear.

**Knowledge depreciates.** Argote, Beckman and Epple studied learning across multiple industrial organisations in a 1990 *Management Science* paper. They found that knowledge acquired through production depreciates rapidly, and that cumulative experience overstates how much an organisation still knows. What a team learned three years ago is not what it knows today.

**Knowledge sits with individuals.** Panopto, a video platform vendor, surveyed 1,000 workers in 2018 and reported that 42% of the institutional knowledge in a role was unique to the person in it. The figure is self-reported and vendor-run, so read it as direction. It matches the experience of anyone who has inherited a function: the shared drive holds the decks, not the reasons.

**Failures go unreported.** Amy Edmondson, writing in *Harvard Business Review* in 2011, asked executives how many of the failures in their organisations were truly blameworthy. They answered 2% to 5%. Asked how many were treated as blameworthy, they said 70% to 90%. Her conclusion was that many failures are never reported and their lessons are lost. An organisation that punishes failure will not write down why things died.

## Not every death is the same

The most useful thing a graveyard record can do is say why something died, because the reasons have very different implications for revival.

**Disproven**: tried properly, with resources, and it did not work. Revive only with new evidence that the conditions have changed.

**Under-tried**: abandoned for lack of time, budget or attention, before it was really tested. These may be good ideas that were never given a fair chance.

**Overtaken**: worked, but was replaced by something better or made redundant by events.

**Political**: stopped because of who sponsored it or who opposed it, not because of its merits.

Many ideas that organisations believe were disproven were actually under-tried. That distinction alone can save a promising idea from permanent burial, and save the organisation from repeating a genuine failure. Edmondson's work gives one reason the confusion is common: her spectrum of failure runs from deliberate deviation at one end to thoughtful experimentation at the other, and she warns that pilots are too often run under optimal conditions rather than representative ones. A pilot that was under-resourced, or run in the wrong conditions, did not disprove anything.

| Classification | Test for it | What revival requires |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Disproven | Ran for its planned period, with its planned resources, against a written threshold | New evidence that a named condition has changed |
| Under-tried | Stopped early, under-funded, or without an owner | The missing resource or owner, stated in advance |
| Overtaken | Worked, then replaced or made redundant | The replacement failing, or the event reversing |
| Political | Stopped by sponsorship or opposition, not results | A sponsor and a fair test |

> Many ideas that organisations believe were disproven were actually under-tried.

## The record

For each abandoned approach: what was tried, for how long, with what resources; what happened; why it was stopped, classified as above; and **what would make it worth trying again**. That last field turns a tombstone into a reopenable option with a stated condition.

| Field | Example entry (illustrative) |
| --- | --- |
| What was tried | Partner referral programme for mid-market accounts |
| Duration and resources | Two quarters, one part-time owner, no budget for partner enablement |
| What happened | Four referrals, one closed |
| Why stopped | Under-tried: owner reassigned in month four |
| Revival condition | A dedicated owner and an enablement budget agreed before relaunch |
| Recorded by, and when | Head of sales, at the quarterly review |

The format is a [decision record](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-decision-record/) with one extra field. The revival condition is what the record of a lost deal is to sales: our explainer on [closed-lost reasons](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-closed-lost-reason/) makes the case that the reason field is the one AI systems most need and CRMs most often leave blank. When conditions change, add a new entry that supersedes the old one rather than editing it; [Supersede, never overwrite](https://lowob.com/research/supersede-never-overwrite/) covers why.

## Surfacing it at the right moment

A graveyard nobody consults is just storage. NASA learned this at some cost. Its Office of Inspector General reviewed the agency's Lessons Learned Information System in March 2012. Of 28 project managers surveyed, 16, or 57%, said they had used the system, and 12, or 43%, had contributed to it. Managers called it outdated, hard to use and short of information relevant to their projects. The agency was spending about three quarters of a million dollars a year on it, and the inspector general questioned whether that was a prudent investment.

The lesson is not that recording fails. It is that an archive which waits to be searched will not be searched. Match new proposals against graveyard records on the situation, not the wording, and surface the match when the proposal is made: "A similar approach was tried in 2025 and stopped after two quarters; classified as under-tried; revival condition: dedicated owner." That one message is often worth more than the rest of the system combined. Supplying comparable past decisions to a model at the moment of a new one is what [decision precedent in AI](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-decision-precedent-in-ai/) describes, and the graveyard is its most valuable source.

The moment of greatest risk is a change of owner. Our piece on [handovers](https://lowob.com/research/handovers-are-where-reasoning-pours-out/) covers why reasoning leaks when people move, and the graveyard should be part of every handover pack.

## What to count

**Repeat failures**: an abandoned approach tried again without new evidence, and failing for the same reason. It should be zero.

**Successful revivals**: graveyard items reopened because their revival condition was met, that then worked. These prove the graveyard is not just a list of reasons to say no.

## In practice

Backfill the graveyard for one function: the ten most significant abandoned initiatives of the last three years. Classify each as disproven, under-tried, overtaken or political, with a revival condition. Match new proposals against it automatically and surface the closest record.

Report repeat failures and successful revivals once a year.

**What would prove this wrong:** Organisations with a maintained graveyard showing no fewer repeat failures, and no more successful revivals, than those without. Then the past is less informative than this piece assumes. We know of no controlled study of graveyard records specifically; the evidence above is on forgetting and on archives, not on this format.

## lowob takeaways

- **Classify every death.** Disproven, under-tried, overtaken or political, because each has different implications for revival.
- **Write the revival condition.** It turns a tombstone into a reopenable option.
- **Push, do not wait.** Surface the closest record when a proposal is made, as NASA's unread archive shows.
- **Count two things.** Repeat failures, which should be zero, and successful revivals.

## Common questions

### How do companies avoid repeating failed initiatives?

Keep a graveyard record of each abandoned approach: what was tried, for how long and with what resources, what happened, why it stopped and what would make it worth trying again. Match new proposals against it and surface the closest record when the proposal is made.

### What is the difference between a disproven idea and an under-tried one?

A disproven idea was tried properly, with resources, and did not work; revive it only with new evidence that conditions changed. An under-tried idea was abandoned for lack of time, budget or attention before it was really tested.

### Why do lessons-learned databases go unused?

They wait to be searched. NASA's inspector general found only 57% of project managers surveyed used the agency's system, citing outdated content and poor relevance. Records need to be pushed at the moment of a related proposal.

### How do you start capturing institutional knowledge about abandoned projects?

Backfill the graveyard for one function with the ten most significant abandoned initiatives of the last three years, classify each, and give each a revival condition.
